title: Making inferences with incomplete epidemiological data: a proof-of-concept estimating measles vaccine coverage across Canada
summary:
Background & aims of study

Current measles outbreaks around the world have highlighted the evolving immunity landscape of some vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs). In Canada, there have been approximately 1,100 reported measles cases between January and June 2026 alone. This far exceeds the previous average annual case counts of <200. This significant outbreak has underscored the need to better understand the present state of population immunity to measles in Canada, an essential input parameter for outbreak response models. Most population immunity in this setting is derived from routine childhood vaccination, but vaccine coverage data is available heterogeneously across the country and is typically collected cross-sectionally to monitor population adherence to immunization schedules rather than to inform population-level susceptibility. This study developed statistical methods to adapt available measles vaccine coverage estimates into more complete estimates of present-day immunity in Canada by age and province/territory (PT).

Methods & results

First, a standardized dataset for vaccine coverage by PT was collated from existing publicly-available datasets and reports. A significant number of vaccine coverage estimates were missing by PT, dose, and year. We used Gaussian Process models to impute current coverage with at least one dose of a measles vaccine, to create a complete 'modelled dataset' by PT and age. Our modelling framework was tested against data for England, which was much more complete, to validate our approach.

Implications

We developed methodology for estimating vaccine coverage in the absence of detailed population immunity data, to support ongoing measles outbreak modelling response work. While this project focused on measles, we built the associated code/tools such that the methodology can be applied to other vaccine-preventable diseases in future outbreak settings.

title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
summary:
Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

Author summary

Humans and animals have to fight influenza virus and other infections without inducing immunopathology. After detection of an infection, the innate immune system produces type I interferon (IFN), a signal that starts a protective response. However, high levels of IFN and prolonged IFN expression can cause damage to tissues and worsen disease. Negative feedback is one route by which IFN production can stop, but its activation during viral infection remains poorly understood. A central question is why viruses can continue to replicate and spread despite a strong IFN response. We here investigated why IFN levels can begin to decline while virus levels continue to rise during influenza virus infection. This decline is most pronounced when the virus produces large amounts of defective viral genomes (DVGs). These defective genomes arise naturally during viral replication and are produced by many RNA viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, Ebola virus, and measles virus. Using cell-culture experiments, computational modelling, and fitting of our model to cell-culture and mouse data, we find that defective genomes contribute to both IFN activation and its negative feedback. Both the experiments and model support a mechanism in which IFN accumulation during infection suppresses its own production, and that this suppression can start earlier under strong DVG stimulation. At the local level, this can allow viral spread to continue even while overall IFN levels remain high. Overall, our findings reveal an additional level of interplay between defective viral genomes and the host innate immune system. They also suggest that the potential therapeutic use of defective genomes must be carefully calibrated to achieve an optimal antiviral response.

title: Socioeconomic and health system determinants of zero-dose and under-immunization among children in Zambia: Evidence from the 2024 Demographic and Health Survey
summary: Despite progress in childhood immunization, Zambia retains pockets of zero-dose children (those who have not received the first dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-containing vaccine, DTP1) and under-immunised children (those missing one or more vaccines in the recommended schedule), sustaining vulnerability to vaccine-preventable diseases. Understanding the factors associated with missed vaccination is essential for achieving Immunization Agenda 2030 targets. We analysed cross-sectional data from 1,738 children aged 12-23 months identified through the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey, a nationally representative survey using a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design. Three outcomes were assessed: zero-dose status (no DTP1), under-immunization by the basic schedule (BCG, DTP1-3, OPV1-3, measles-1), and under-immunization by the national expanded schedule (basic plus PCV1-3 and rotavirus1-2). Survey-weighted multivariable regression identified associated factors. Nationally, 3.2% (95% CI: 2.1-4.3%) of children were zero-dose, 36.1% (95% CI: 33.0-39.2%) were under-immunised by the basic schedule, and 69.9% (95% CI: 67.0-72.8%) by the national schedule. Zero-dose prevalence ranged tenfold across provinces, from 0.6% in Lusaka to 6.9% in North Western. In adjusted models, children in the richest households had 93% lower odds of zero-dose than the poorest (aOR 0.07, 95% CI: 0.02-0.29). Facility delivery reduced zero-dose by 68% (aOR 0.32, 95% CI: 0.15-0.69). For basic-schedule under-immunization, secondary education (aOR 0.50, 95% CI: 0.30-0.82; prevalence ratio 0.68) and vaccination card possession (aOR 0.24, 95% CI: 0.14-0.40; prevalence ratio 0.53) were associated with lower odds. Wealth effects differed significantly by residence for all outcomes (p < 0.001). Zero-dose and under-immunization in Zambia are profoundly socioeconomically and geographically patterned. Reaching zero-dose children requires targeting the poorest households and those with home deliveries, particularly in North Western and Northern provinces. Improving vaccination card coverage may reduce broader under-immunization. Gaps in national schedule coverage are consistent with supply-side constraints requiring structural health system responses, though direct supply-side measurement was beyond the scope of this analysis.

title: [Fifty years of vaccination in Spain: evolution, achievements and challenges for Public Health]
summary: Vaccination has been one of the most effective public health strategies in Spain, evolving from isolated campaigns to the implementation of a common vaccination schedule. Initiated in 1975 with seven basic vaccines, the schedule was progressively consolidated, culminating in the 2018 approval of a unified calendar agreed upon by the Ministry of Health and the autonomous communities. This model has maintained very high childhood vaccination coverage and has contributed to smallpox eradication, the elimination of polio and rubella, and the maintenance of measles elimination for several years. Its success relies on interterritorial governance, evidence-based and ethical decision-making, and robust epidemiological surveillance. Despite these achievements, important challenges remain: coverage gaps between doses and age groups; territorial and organizational variability; incomplete vaccination in part of the adult population; vaccine hesitancy; and the sustainability of the schedule as new interventions are introduced. The recent measles situation also reinforces the need to close immunity gaps and maintain sensitive epidemiological and microbiological surveillance. The current approach promotes lifelong immunization, including adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. Technologies such as mRNA vaccines and genomic surveillance offer new possibilities. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the need for strong international coordination and community engagement. Thus, the common vaccination schedule stands as a pillar of healthcare cohesion, and its future depends on political consensus, scientific innovation, and equity.

title: Determinants of Measles Vaccine Failure and Breakthrough Infections: A Systematic Review of IgG Avidity Based Immunological Markers and Host Genetic Polymorphisms
summary:
Background

Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, despite high reported coverage. Determinants of measles vaccine failure remain incompletely characterized.

Methods

Five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library) were searched from inception. Studies in vaccinated individuals evaluating IgG avidity markers or host genetic polymorphisms were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, JBI checklist and modified HuGENet framework. Findings were synthesized narratively (PROSPERO: CRD420261415732).

Results

Sixteen studies (8169 participants; 1998-2025) met inclusion criteria. Across seven studies with event-level data, primary vaccine failure ranged from 24.2% to 90.8%. Reproducible host genetic associations were observed for HLA Class I/II alleles, measles receptor genes (SLAM/CD150, CD46, CD209), TLR pathway genes, antiviral effector genes and cytokine/cytokine receptor genes. No study reported extractable breakthrough infection or dichotomous IgG avidity data.

Conclusion

Reproducible host genetic determinants of measles antibody response cluster at HLA loci, the measles receptor axis and the TLR pathway. Inconsistent definitions and absent standardized reporting preclude firm conclusions. Prospective harmonized studies are required.

title: Predictors of severe measles outcomes in hospitalized patients in Jerusalem, 2025
summary:
Objectives

Measles is a vaccine-preventable disease. Defining risk factors for poor outcomes in hospitalized patients can improve future measles outbreak preparedness.

Methods

Data were collected on all confirmed measles cases that were evaluated at one of the emergency departments (ED) in the three main hospitals in Jerusalem from the first reported case of the current outbreak on April 10th to December 31st, 2025. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were analyzed using robust Poisson multivariable models to calculate incidence rate ratios (IRR) for hospitalization, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and death.

Results

Among 786 individuals who visited the ED with confirmed measles, the rates of hospital admission (≥1 day), ICU, ECMO and death were 83.4%, 6.4%, 0.8%, and 1.4%, respectively. Complete data were available for 567 patients, of whom 303 (53.4%) were males. Median age was 2.1 years (IQR 1.2-3.8), and 474 (83.6%) were younger than 5 years. Most patients were unvaccinated (91.0%). Secondary infections were frequent, including lobar pneumonia (28.7%) and community-acquired bacteremia (3.5%). Respiratory support and severe dehydration were associated with hospital admission (IRR 1.4, 95% CI 1.3-1.5; p<0.001 and 9.5, 4.8-18.4; p<0.001, respectively) and ICU admission (IRR 1.3, 1.2-1.4; p<0.001 and 5.2, 2.1-12.4; p<0.001, respectively). Community-acquired bacteremia was associated with death or ECMO (IRR 44.5, 12.5-158.6; p<0.001).

Conclusions

Despite high access to medical care in this urban setting, measles caused substantial morbidity and mortality. Respiratory compromise, severe dehydration, and bacteremia identified patients at increased risk of severe outcomes.

title: Impact of a large measles outbreak associated with transmission in the Americas and Canada's loss of measles elimination status: descriptive cohort study
summary:
Objective

To describe the epidemiological characteristics, public health response, and evidence of international spread of a large measles outbreak that contributed to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status.

Design

Descriptive analysis of the cohort of measles outbreak cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period: epidemiological week of 28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025.

Setting

Ontario, Canada.

Participants

Individuals meeting the outbreak case definition for confirmed or probable measles infection during the outbreak period.

Exposure

Exposure to measles virus associated with the Ontario outbreak and related transmission chains.

Main outcome measures

Demographic characteristics, vaccination status, admission to hospital, complications, pregnancy associated outcomes, mortality, and evidence of international spread based on measles virus genotyping and sequencing. Cases were identified using an outbreak-specific case definition incorporating epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, and viral sequencing criteria. Phylogenetic analysis of measles virus sequences was used to assess evidence of onwards spread to other countries.

Results

The outbreak consisted of 2377 cases (2064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks and contributed to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status. Most cases (2146/2377, 90.3%) occurred among members of historically under-vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2377 cases, approximately three quarters of cases (n=1736, 73.0%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2121 (89.2%) were unvaccinated, and 97 (4.1%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 (7%) admissions to hospital, 13 (<1%) admissions to intensive care unit, 51 (2.1%) infections during pregnancy, 10 (<1%) congenital measles infections, one (<1%) case of encephalitis, and one (<1%) infant death. Sequencing identified a novel N450 distinct sequence identifier that was subsequently detected in countries including the United States of America, Mexico, and the Netherlands. The outbreak strain was designated a World Health Organization named strain (MVs/Ontario.CAN/47.24).

Conclusions

These findings highlight the risk of measles re-establishment in countries that have attained elimination and underscore the importance of culturally appropriate community engagement to build trust in immunisation and prevent future outbreaks. This outbreak shows the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of long standing immunity gaps within interconnected communities across the Americas and the population-level protection that limited broader community transmission.

title: Factors Associated with Length of Hospital Stay and Clinical Characteristics of Children Hospitalized with Measles
summary:
Objective

To evaluate the clinical characteristics, complications, and factors associated with the length of hospital stay in children hospitalized with measles.

Materials and methods

This retrospective, observational study included children aged 0-18 years hospitalized with measles between January and December 2023 at a tertiary care center in Istanbul, Türkiye. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and hospitalization data were analyzed.

Results

Sixty-one hospitalized children with measles were included; 32 (52.5%) were younger than 5 years and 29 (47.5%) were older than 5 years. Fifty-nine percent were Turkish citizens, 41% were foreign nationals, and 57.4% were male. Overall, 77% were unvaccinated. Fever and rash were present in all patients. Pneumonia was the most common complication (68.9%), followed by hepatitis (11.5%), gingivostomatitis (11.5%), ocular complications (9.8%), and otitis (4.9%). All hepatitis cases occurred in children older than 5 years. Three patients (5.2%) required pediatric intensive care. In univariable linear regression analyses, pneumonia/bronchopneumonia, C-reactive protein (CRP), and white blood cell count were significantly associated with longer hospital stay. In the primary multivariable linear regression model, only CRP remained independently associated with prolonged hospitalization (B = 0.017, 95% CI = 0.0002-0.0333; P = .047). No measles-related deaths occurred.

Conclusion

Measles remains a major public health problem, particularly among unvaccinated children. Inflammatory markers were associated with prolonged hospitalization, suggesting that systemic inflammation may contribute to longer inpatient care. Larger multicenter studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Overcoming glioma heterogeneity: Strategies to improve the specificity of oncolytic viruses
summary: High-grade gliomas remain difficult to treat because of their infiltrative growth, cellular heterogeneity, and resistance to conventional therapies. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) offer a therapeutic approach that combines preferential viral replication in malignant cells with activation of antitumor immunity. However, heterogeneous receptor expression, intracellular antiviral defenses, limited intratumoral distribution, and central nervous system safety constraints complicate clinical translation. This review examines how genetic, transcriptional, metabolic, epigenetic, and immune heterogeneity influence viral entry, replication, dissemination, and therapeutic activity in glioma. We compare established and emerging platforms, including adenovirus, herpes simplex viruses, PVSRIPO, measles virus, vaccinia virus, and M1 alphavirus, while distinguishing preclinical findings from clinical evidence. We also discuss approaches to tumor selectivity, delivery, immune microenvironment remodeling, and combination checkpoint blockade. Clinical studies demonstrate feasibility and occasional durable responses, but most are small and uncontrolled, and early activity has not consistently translated into benefit in larger trials. Progress requires platform-specific biomarkers, representative experimental models, rigorous neurological safety assessment, and controlled clinical evaluation. Improving specificity must therefore be considered together with tumor coverage, immune function, and clinically meaningful outcomes.

title: Childhood vaccination timeliness, under-immunization-for-age and measles effective immunity in Peru: a province and birth-cohort analysis of national survey data, 2004-2025
summary:
Background

Using the survey rounds 2004-2025 of Peru's Demographic and Family Health Survey (ENDES) for children aged 12-35 months, we estimated the timeliness of sentinel vaccine doses; under-immunization-for-age and late receipt by province and birth cohort; and the gap between the proportion of children effectively immune to measles and the herd-immunity threshold.

Methods

Pooled cross-sections were analysed. Timeliness was measured in days, within World Health Organization age bands, among children whose vaccination card was seen; weighting and bounds addressed selection. We estimated the share of the maternal-education gap in timeliness running through antenatal and delivery care and fitted Bayesian small-area models for 196 provinces.

Results

Among card-seen children, on-time receipt was 86.8% for bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG), 65.3% for the third dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP)-containing vaccine (DTP3), 61.1% for the first measles-containing dose and, in survey rounds 2015-2025, 39.2% for the second. For all children in the age band, recall-based bounds put DTP3 timeliness at 54.5%-63.5%, below the card-seen estimate. Children of more educated mothers had a 6.7-point lower risk of DTP3 not on time; under stated assumptions, antenatal care and institutional delivery explained 0.85 points (13%) of this gap. In the 2020-2025 birth cohort, 28 provinces were classed worse than the national level for DTP3 not on time. In the 2020-2024 birth cohort, the province-average proportion of children effectively immune to measles was 89.8%, below the herd-immunity thresholds for a basic reproduction number (R0) of 15-18; for R0 = 12, the average probability that a province fell below the threshold was 59.9%.

Conclusions

Many card-seen children were vaccinated late, and card-based estimates probably overstate DTP3 timeliness. Under the assumed vaccine effectiveness and R0 of 15-18, measles immunity stayed below herd-immunity thresholds.

title: Measles transmission-related epidemiological parameter estimates: a systematic review and meta-analysis
summary: With the recent resurgence of global measles outbreaks, it is crucial to understand measles transmission dynamics to guide timely and effective public health responses and parameterize infectious disease models for accurate outbreak projections. This systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive resource of measles transmission-related epidemiological parameters. A search was conducted from inception to 14 May 2024. English and French primary studies of transmission-related epidemiological parameters were included, and standard systematic review methodology was followed. Evidence was synthesized using random-effects meta-analyses and descriptive plots. Subgroup analyses by World Health Organization (WHO) region, population, decade, and quality of reporting were conducted to explore heterogeneity. Between 1910 and 2024, 1 209 estimates across 32 transmission-related epidemiological parameters from 612 studies were reported. Measles was characterized by a pooled incubation period (13.5 days, 95%CI 12.6-14.4; I<sup>2</sup> = 95.9%), serial interval (12.4 days, 95%CI 11.5-13.4; I<sup>2</sup> = 97.6%), symptom onset to hospitalization (4.8 days, 95%CI 3.7-5.8, I<sup>2</sup> = 99.7%), and basic reproduction number median 11.5 (range of 0-57). This work is part of a global epidemic preparedness and response project to establish an accessible living Global Repository of Epidemiological Parameters aimed at reducing duplicative efforts in identifying and summarizing epidemiological parameters.

title: Spatio-temporal dynamics, transmission hotspots, and vaccination gaps driving measles persistence in Nigeria, 2006-2025
summary: Measles remains a major public health concern in Nigeria, contributing disproportionately to the global burden. Persistence of the disease is driven by sub-optimal vaccination coverage and heterogeneous transmission patterns, but the specific spatio-temporal dynamics and the quantitative impact of vaccination gaps at the sub-national level are not fully characterized. This study aimed to provide a comprehensive analysis of measles transmission in Nigeria from 2006 to 2025, with the specific objectives to identify spatial hotspots, quantify their temporal persistence, and evaluate the association between MCV1/MCV2 coverage and measles case ratio. We conducted a national retrospective ecological study, integrating 19 years of surveillance data (2006-2025) and geospatial information, with a focused 4-year analysis of vaccination records (2021-2024). Analytical methods included time-series decomposition, spatial autocorrelation (Local Moran's I and Getis-Ord Gi*), and linear mixed-effects modeling to quantify vaccination effects while accounting for state-level heterogeneity. Analysis of 253,595 measles cases revealed a highly clustered geographic distribution, with 86.4% of the national burden concentrated in northern Nigeria. We identified 38 persistent hotspot Local Government Areas that accounted for 23.2% of all cases. Vaccination coverage was low and disparate, with national averages of 73.8% for MCV1 and 38.4% for MCV2. Mixed-effects modeling confirmed a significant negative association between MCV1 coverage and the measles case ratio, while MCV2 coverage did not show a statistically significant independent effect. Measles transmission in Nigeria is driven by entrenched hotspots in the north and critical vaccination gaps threatening disease resurgence in the south. Achieving elimination requires a tailored strategy: intensive supplemental immunization activities and RI strengthening aimed at reducing endemic transmission in the northern hotspots, coupled with focused efforts to close routine immunization gaps in specific southern states.

title: Acute measles encephalitis in adults: a case series in Vietnam
summary:
Background

Acute measles encephalitis is a rare but severe complication of measles, particularly in adults, and carries high mortality and a substantial risk of neurological sequelae. Two mechanisms are recognized: direct viral invasion of the brain, termed primary measles encephalitis, and an immune-mediated postinfectious process, termed acute postinfectious measles encephalitis. Most descriptions come from children, and the presentation, pathogenesis, and management of adult disease remain poorly defined.

Case presentation

We describe four adults (aged 34-45 years) admitted with fever, rash, and altered mental status. Acute measles infection was confirmed by serum measles-specific IgM or measles virus RNA on real-time reverse-transcription PCR. Measles virus RNA was detected in cerebrospinal fluid in Case 1, indicating primary measles encephalitis. Case 2 was initially mistaken for varicella because of an atypical vesicular rash. Case 3 developed quadriparesis and sphincter dysfunction with electromyographic evidence of bilateral S1 radiculopathy; spinal imaging was not performed. Case 4 showed progressive thalamic and temporal lesions on magnetic resonance imaging. Cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis ranged from 57 to 1046 cells/µL, and improved in most patients within 3 days of intravenous immunoglobulin. Two patients recovered without neurological sequelae, one survived with residual deficits, and one died from persistent cerebral injury complicated by multidrug-resistant septic shock.

Conclusions

In adults, acute measles encephalitis may reflect a biphasic process that combines direct viral neuroinvasion with immune-mediated inflammation, rather than a purely postinfectious phenomenon. Intravenous immunoglobulin was temporally associated with clinical and biochemical improvement, but its therapeutic role cannot be established from a case series and requires controlled study.

title: Domestic Measles Importations in Washington State, January 2026

title: Post-Measles Complications and Mortality in Children under Five Years in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Narrative Review
summary: Background: Global measles vaccination programs have achieved significant reductions in measles-related mortality, with World Health Organization (WHO)-led initiatives expanding vaccine coverage to over 85% of children worldwide. Despite this progress, measles elimination remains elusive, undermined by anti-vaccine sentiment, armed conflicts, migration, refugee crises, and post-COVID-19 disruptions. No WHO region has achieved or sustained measles elimination status since the COVID-19 pandemic, and elimination remains challenging in resource-limited and conflict-affected contexts. A critical yet underappreciated consequence of this ongoing burden is the rise of post-measles complications (PMCs). Vaccine-preventable diseases and malnutrition constitute two critical global health priorities; PMCs represent an important intersection of these agendas that warrant greater attention within the global health framework. Objectives: To review and synthesize current epidemiological evidence on PMCs, examine their pathogenesis, and understand the need for integrated post-measles care strategies in vulnerable populations. Methods: This narrative review included all papers that published primary data on any of the PMCs in the last 55 years, identified through PubMed and Google Scholar. Findings: Epidemiological data show that 30-40% of measles cases in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) develop complications, including pneumonia, diarrhea, otitis media, and, less commonly, encephalitis and ocular disease. PMCs are frequently misattributed to independent illnesses because they often emerge after a delay following the acute infection. Compounding this, measles-induced immune amnesia renders affected individuals vulnerable to secondary infections for up to 2-3 years post-infection. In LMICs and conflict-affected settings, this prolonged immunological vulnerability intersects with pre-existing risk factors such as malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and poor healthcare access, which amplify the consequences substantially. Conclusions: As measles cases resurge globally, the associated burden of PMCs is expected to increase correspondingly. Where PMCs represent a pressing, underaddressed concern, integrated post-measles care strategies are urgently needed from a global health perspective, especially in resource-limited and conflict-affected settings.

title: Estimating the incidence and duration of diagnostic delays for measles
summary:
Objective

Although measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, cases have increased in recent years. Our goal was to estimate the incidence and duration of diagnostic delays for measles and identify factors associated with delays.

Design

Case-crossover.

Setting

We used the Merative MarketScan Research Databases (2001-2023).

Patients

We identified measles cases and evaluated prior healthcare encounters for potential missed diagnostic opportunities.

Methods

Using a bootstrapping approach, we estimated the number of healthcare visits representing possible missed opportunities to diagnose measles during a two-week period preceding the index diagnosis. We utilized Firth logistic regression to assess factors associated with delays.

Results

We identified 4,651 measles cases. During the two-week period prior to diagnosis, 426 (9.2%) patients had healthcare visits with signs or symptoms commonly associated with measles. We estimated 381 (95%CI: 330-440) missed opportunities to diagnose measles. Delays occurred most frequently in outpatient settings (81.0%). Approximately 6.9% (95%CI: 6.1-8.0%) of patients experienced at least one missed opportunity, with a mean delay of 4.05 days (95%CI: 3.48-4.51) (median delay = 2.94 days [95%CI: 2.00-3.00]). An estimated 1.7% (95%CI: 1.1-2.2%) of patients experienced a diagnostic delay lasting a week or longer. Factors associated with an increased likelihood of delays included age <2 years and receiving antibiotic prescriptions.

Conclusions

Diagnostic delays for measles are not uncommon and may facilitate transmission, especially in outpatient settings.

title: Germicidal ultraviolet to reduce transmission of respiratory infections indoors: a systematic review
summary:
Background

Respiratory infections that transmit through air contribute substantially to global morbidity and mortality. Although preclinical data on germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) for air treatment are promising, its real-world effectiveness remains incompletely understood.

Purpose

Review effectiveness and safety of GUV for preventing respiratory infection transmission.

Data sources

Medline, Embase, Global Health, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, Engineering Village, Epistemonikos, Scopus, and Environmental Science Collection from inception through December 2025.

Study selection

Studies of GUV with a comparator, measuring human outcomes including respiratory infections, absenteeism, or adverse events.

Data extraction

At least two investigators extracted data.

Data synthesis

We identified 57 reports describing 40 studies published between 1940 and 2025: 30 non-randomized controlled trials, 4 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), 4 case series, 1 cohort study, and 1 cross-sectional study. Non-randomized studies indicated GUV reduces infections with high transmissibility through air (measles and chickenpox), although results were mixed for undifferentiated respiratory illnesses and absenteeism. Two RCTs were inconclusive or showed only modest effects. Safety monitoring in 16 studies identified no increased eye or skin irritation from properly installed GUV. All studies had at least one threat to validity; 89% were non-randomized, and 83% lacked statistical power calculations.

Limitations

Heterogeneous study designs, interventions, and outcomes precluded meta-analysis.

Conclusions

Several older clinical studies indicated that GUV reduces infections with high transmissibility through air, but its broader effectiveness against respiratory infection remains uncertain. Inconclusive results may reflect methodological and epidemiological limitations rather than true ineffectiveness. Adequately powered RCTs with robust clinical endpoints are needed.

title: Characterizing the relative strength of metapopulation dynamics in measles persistence
summary:
Background/Aims

Measles is a highly infectious, vaccine-preventable disease that remains persistent across much of the world despite continued large-scale control efforts. Local dynamics of measles are shaped by births of susceptible individuals and seasonal drivers of transmission, while broader regional dynamics are shaped by population mobility and metapopulation connectivity. Incidence data, useful for tracking the progress of measles control, are frequently reported only at the aggregate level (e.g., states/provinces), and persistence at this scale may arise because of the independent persistence in all local sub-units or because of regional metapopulation dynamics. Disentangling the contribution of local versus regional persistence is critical in identifying effective strategies for control.

Methods/Results

We show, as vaccination reduces local measles prevalence, metapopulation colonization and extinction events dominate regional persistence. This manifests as a change in the seasonal distribution of cases throughout the year; incidence becomes more uniformly distributed through the year even with no change in underlying seasonal drivers. We demonstrate this using: 1) a seasonally forced, stochastic metapopulation compartmental model; 2) historical measles incidence in the USA; and 3) recent subnational-level measles incidence in Nigeria. We create a novel, scale-free measure to quantify the contribution of metapopulation dynamics to persistence, roundness, defined as the geometric mean of the scaled maximum and minimum monthly incidence. A low value of roundness indicates strong local persistence dominated by the seasonal attractor, while a high value indicates strong metapopulation persistence. We illustrate the properties of this measure using simulations and observed data. In the USA, roundness nearly doubled after the introduction of the measles-containing vaccine. In Nigeria, roundness is well correlated with observed vaccine coverage, with a Pearson’s r of 0.70 (95% CI: 0.57, 0.80), discriminating between northern states dominated by local persistence of measles and southern states where persistence is maintained by regional dynamics.

Conclusion

Identifying how measles persists is important in its control—vaccination strategies may differ if persistence is largely local, or if persistence is driven by connectivity from surrounding areas, even where yearly incidence is comparable. Our approach can be valuable areas where other measures (connectivity, mobility, laboratory confirmed illness) are not widely available.

title: Palmoplantar Maculopapular Rash Mimicking Secondary Syphilis in Infectious Mononucleosis After Sequential Antibiotic Exposure: A Case Report
summary: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) commonly presents with pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and fever. Cutaneous eruptions may occur, particularly following antibiotic exposure. We report a case of a man in his late 20s who developed a widespread maculopapular rash following sequential exposure to multiple antibiotics in the setting of acute EBV infection. The rash progressed to involve the palms and soles, raising concern for secondary syphilis and a possible drug hypersensitivity reaction. Investigations demonstrated marked lymphocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers and deranged liver enzymes. Throat culture was negative for beta-haemolytic streptococci and the antistreptolysin O titre did not suggest recent streptococcal infection. Treponema pallidum antibody testing and measles polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were negative. Subsequent EBV PCR and repeat serology supported acute EBV infection. The patient improved with conservative management, with resolution of the rash and normalization of the white cell count and liver enzymes at follow-up. Retrospective review also identified prior intravenous amoxicillin exposure during admission for appendicitis, adding further uncertainty regarding the cause of the eruption. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of rash occurring during acute EBV infection following multiple antibiotic exposures and the importance of considering both EBV-associated exanthem and drug hypersensitivity in the differential diagnosis. Accurate assessment of suspected penicillin allergy is important to guide future antibiotic prescribing.

title: Precision Oncology: Cancer Specialists' Perspectives on Molecular Profiling, Targeted Therapy, and Barriers to Access
summary:
Background

Precision oncology has transformed cancer care through molecular profiling and biomarker-guided therapies. However, access remains uneven in resource-constrained settings. In Bangladesh, quantitative evidence characterizing barriers to molecular profiling and targeted therapy remains limited, particularly regarding barriers beyond financial constraints. This study aims to describe oncologists' perspective regarding current molecular profiling practices and receipt of targeted therapy among eligible patients, and to identify major financial and non-financial barriers and potential strategies for improving access to precision oncology as perceived by the physicians.

Methods

A nationwide cross-sectional survey was conducted from June to July 2026 among cancer specialists actively involved in cancer care in Bangladesh. A structured questionnaire assessed molecular profiling and targeted therapy practices, perceived barriers, and potential strategies for improving access. Data from 52 respondents were analyzed descriptively using frequencies and percentages.

Results

Molecular profiling was recommended often or always by 27 (51.9%) respondents. estrogen receptor/progesterone receptor/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (ER/PR/HER2) (90.4%), microsatellite instability/mismatch repair (MSI/MMR) (82.7%), and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) (80.8%) were the most requested molecular tests. However, 45 (86.5%) respondents reported that no more than 25% of eligible patients ultimately received targeted therapy. High cost of targeted therapy was rated as a major or very major barrier by 46 (88.5%) respondents, followed by high cost of molecular testing (45, 86.5%). Among non-financial barriers, limited testing facilities (29, 55.8%), limited patient understanding or acceptance of molecular testing (28, 53.8%), and long turnaround time for molecular testing results (25, 48.1%) were most frequently rated as major or very major barriers. Most respondents (42, 80.8%) agreed or strongly agreed that targeted therapy should become standard practice in Bangladesh where indicated. Reduced testing costs (43, 82.7%) and government-subsidized insurance coverage (33, 63.5%) were the most frequently selected strategies for improving access.

Conclusion

Cancer specialists in Bangladesh reported substantial use of molecular profiling but limited receipt of targeted therapy among eligible patients. Although financial constraints emerged as the most prominent barriers, important non-financial challenges related to testing infrastructure, patient understanding and acceptance, and turnaround time were also identified. In the context of limited existing quantitative evidence from Bangladesh, these findings provide initial insight into the relative prominence of financial and non-financial barriers and may inform strategies to improve access to precision oncology.

title: Combating Infectious Disease Challenges: Have We Gone Twenty Steps Forward or Backward?
summary: The 2025 webinar: "Combating Infectious Disease Challenges: Have We Gone Twenty Steps Forward or Backward?" explores the need for a paradigm shift in public health strategies to address airborne pathogens. Despite growing awareness, many health care systems still underestimate the complexity of airborne transmission, relying on surgical masks for protection against airborne pathogens and on outdated assumptions that aerosol-generating procedures are required to spread them. Evidence shows that pathogens can be aerosolized through Aerosol-Generating-Activities (AGA), which are undertaken every day, such as breathing, talking, and singing, necessitating the use of respirators (eg, N95 masks), airborne infection isolation rooms, and improved indoor air quality. Upgrading HVAC systems and maintaining indoor CO2 levels below 800 ppm are critical steps toward safer environments. The importance of One Health was highlighted by a discussion of H5N1, including its impact on our food supply and its potential to mutate, which could allow sustained human-to-human transmission. Vaccination remains a cornerstone of infectious disease prevention, credited with saving an estimated 154 million lives globally over the past 5 decades. However, misinformation continues to erode public trust, with nearly 25% of Americans believing the MMR vaccine may cause autism-threatening herd immunity for diseases like measles. The webinar also highlights the importance of elimination strategies at the onset of pandemics. While such approaches were effective against MERS and SARS-CoV-1, they failed against SARS-CoV-2. A failure associated with implementation delays and insufficient infrastructure. This webinar underscores the need for evidence-based interventions, public education, and systemic reform to better prepare for future infectious disease threats.

title: First evidence of measles virus detected from exhaled breath in humans
summary:
Objectives

Measles is among the most transmissible human infections, yet direct capture of measles virus from an infected person's exhaled breath has not been described. We assessed whether measles virus RNA can be detected from exhaled breath using facemask sampling (FMS).

Methods

We studied a 23-year-old unvaccinated woman with laboratory-confirmed measles (throat-swab RT-qPCR positive on day 5 post symptom onset). From day 10 post symptom onset, longitudinal sampling was performed for six consecutive days with duplicate specimens collected at each timepoint from the throat, face, cutaneous lesions and exhaled breath using a surgical mask fitted with polyvinyl alcohol sampling strips (FMS). Dissolved mask strips and swab eluates underwent RNA extraction followed by RT-qPCR targeting measles nucleoprotein and haemagglutinin genes, with human RNase P as a sample adequacy control. Quantification was derived from nucleoprotein-gene standards and normalised per strip or per 100 μL of swab eluate.

Results

Measles virus RNA was consistently detected in exhaled breath captured by FMS and remained >10ˆ4 genome copies per sampling strip despite sampling beginning 10 days after symptom onset. During FMS collection, the participant reported no respiratory symptoms and did not vocalise. RNA kinetics differed by sampling site: throat and facial swabs increased even after complete rash resolution, whereas cutaneous-lesion swabs yielded comparatively low RNA levels. FMS kinetics diverged from throat swabs over time, suggesting distinct patterns of virus emission across compartments.

Conclusions

This study provides the first empirical evidence that measles virus RNA can be captured directly from the exhaled breath of an individual with measles. Although RNA detection does not confirm infectious virus, persistent high-level exhaled RNA supports FMS as a practical, non-invasive tool to study measles respiratory emission and may inform understanding of transmission and the duration of potential contagiousness. Empirical sampling of different respiratory compartments may help refine infection-prevention guidance during resurgent outbreaks.

title: Seroprevalence of measles virus antibodies among residents of Kavaratti, Lakshadweep: assessing the immunity gap
summary: Despite India's progress toward measles elimination, serological data from isolated communities such as Lakshadweep remain limited. title: Comparative analysis of central nervous system persistence of morbilliviruses across host species reveals shared features with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
summary:
Background

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare but always fatal neurological complication of measles, associated with persistent measles virus (MeV) infection of the central nervous system (CNS). MeV is detected in the brains of deceased SSPE patients as hypermutated viral genomes, which often contain premature stop codons in the matrix (M) gene and encode a hyperfusogenic fusion (F) protein. As a result, infected cells in the CNS cannot produce virions but rather transmit the viral ribonucleoprotein from cell-to-cell in a slow but progressive manner, which ultimately results in widespread MeV infection of the brain. However, our understanding of the pathogenesis of SSPE is constrained by the lack of animal models combined with a clinically silent incubation period of several years.

Main text

In a recent publication in PNAS, Daniel Roji et al. analysed animal morbillivirus sequences detected in the brains of persistently infected hosts, including a lynx (canine distemper virus, CDV), two seals (phocine distemper virus, PDV) and a dolphin (cetacean morbillivirus, CeMV). The authors describe that the morbillivirus sequences detected in these animals contained unique mutational signatures. The CDV, CeMV and one of the PDV sequences encoded nonfunctional M proteins and hyperfusogenic F proteins, reminiscent of the mutational profile of MeV detected in SSPE patients. Therefore, the authors conclude that human and animal morbilliviruses associated with chronic neurological infections share key genotypic and phenotypic traits, and that thorough analysis of naturally occurring animal morbillivirus infections could improve our understanding of SSPE pathogenesis.

Conclusion

The comparison of neurological complications associated with human and animal morbillivirus infections as described by Daniel Roji et al. provides a unique One Health approach to understanding the drivers of SSPE. These findings may support the development of early diagnostics or an animal model for SSPE, providing an opportunity to test novel intervention strategies.

title: The herd immunity attractor: selection, drift, and the steady-state undersupply of vaccination in 195 countries, 1980-2025
summary: Vaccination is the canonical positive externality in health economics: because each vaccination protects others, decentralized choice is predicted to stall below the herd immunity threshold. Yet little evidence exists on the law of motion that governs national coverage. This study estimates it directly. I model the vaccinate-or-not decision of a heterogeneous household population as an expected-utility problem whose net payoff declines in the vaccinated share, aggregate it through an explicit revision protocol into a selection-mutation (replicator-mutator) equation in which payoff-responsive switching coexists with health-system contact and attrition hazards, and estimate the resulting equation on the World Health Organization/United Nations Children's Fund (WHO/UNICEF) Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC, 2025 revision) for 195 countries over 1980-2025, with UN cohort denominators and World Bank income and health-system capacity controls. An exact identification result shows that the linear turnover coefficient equals the difference between the law of motion at full and at zero coverage, so it is identified from boundary observations independently of the payoff parameters, whereas the payoff slope is identified only where coverage traverses the simplex. First, in the interior of the coverage range, the dynamics are dominated by a strong linear restoring force, implying an annual turnover of 15%-25% of the relevant pool; the payoff slope is statistically weak there, and interior data cannot distinguish institutional flows from payoff-insensitive revision, so the estimated hazards bound the institutional component from above. Second, the free-riding signature appears where it is identified: sharply in the Hib rollout, which spans the full coverage range, and weakly on the first-dose DTP margin. Third, every country's law of motion has a stable interior rest point; the births-weighted world rest point for first-dose measles vaccination is 78%, below the 92%-94% herd band; 74% of countries rest below it, and a coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) era shift lowered the median rest point by 3.3 points. Because the leverage of retention over payoff instruments equals 1/(1 - x *) under the replicator protocol and diverges along the last mile under any smooth, bounded choice protocol, closing the gap is a default-and-retention problem rather than a price problem.

title: Global and regional burden of measles and vaccine coverage among children under 5 years, 1990-2023: a Global Burden of Disease Study
summary: Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable burden among children, particularly in low-income settings. Despite decades of progress, there are indications of measles resurgence due to stagnation in vaccine coverage. Here, using the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, we systematically assessed measles incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and vaccine coverage (measles-containing vaccine 1 (MCV1) and measles-containing vaccine 2 (MCV2)) among children under 5 years of age across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Between 1990 and 2019, global measles incidence and mortality declined by approximately 80% and 90%, respectively, but rebounded sharply after 2020, with 15.6 million cases and 118,000 deaths estimated in 2023 (+40% and +12% increases, respectively, between 2019 and 2023). Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia continue to bear the highest burden. Global MCV1 coverage rose from 67.2% in 1990 to 83.6% in 2019 but stalled and declined slightly to 81.0% by 2023; MCV2 coverage increased from 14.4% in 1990 to 68.4% in 2019 and reached 71.4% by 2023. Several regions remain well below the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030) target of 90% coverage. The recent measles resurgence underscores the fragility of global immunization progress and the urgent need to restore routine vaccination, close immunity gaps and strengthen outbreak preparedness.

title: Immunopathogenetic Features of Measles in Adults: Association of Vaccination Status with Measles-Specific IgM Levels and Cytokine Profile (IL-1β, IL-10)
summary: The influence of prior measles vaccination on humoral and cytokine immune responses during acute measles in adults remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated measles-specific IgM antibody levels, the early dynamics of interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-10, and their associations with hematological parameters according to documented vaccination status. This single-center observational study included 80 adults with clinically compatible measles and positive measles-specific IgM results who were hospitalized 3-5 days after disease onset with moderate or severe illness. Patients were classified as having documented prior measles vaccination (n = 40) or no documented evidence of prior measles vaccination (n = 40). Measles-specific IgM antibodies were measured by ELISA on day 7 after rash onset. Serum IL-1β, IL-10, total leukocyte count, and relative lymphocyte percentage were assessed at admission and on day 3 of hospitalization. Non-parametric statistical methods were applied for group comparisons and correlation analyses. An additional regression analysis was performed to assess between-group differences in IL-10 after adjustment for disease severity. Patients with documented vaccination had significantly higher measles-specific IgM levels. IL-1β decreased and IL-10 increased significantly from admission to day 3 in both groups, with no between-group differences in IL-1β. In unadjusted analyses, IL-10 was higher in patients without documented vaccination at both time points. After adjustment for disease severity, the IL-10 difference at admission was no longer significant, whereas the difference on day 3 remained significant. Strong positive correlations between IL-1β and IL-10 were observed in both groups, while IgM correlated positively with relative lymphocyte percentage in patients without documented vaccination. Documented prior measles vaccination was associated with higher measles-specific IgM levels, while the between-group difference in IL-10 on day 3 persisted after adjustment for disease severity. IL-1β dynamics were similar between the groups. These findings demonstrate differences in immune-response patterns between adults with documented prior measles vaccination and those without documented evidence of vaccination, while supporting cautious interpretation of these associations.

title: Analytical validation of MethyLiverDx-Sigma, a plasma cfDNA methylation assay for hepatocellular carcinoma detection
summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance relies on ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein, both limited in sensitivity for early-stage disease; aberrant methylation of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) offers a promising blood-based approach. Reported here is the analytical validation of MethyLiverDx-Sigma (MLDx-s), an assay that detects methylated RNF135 and DNMT3A in bisulfite-converted plasma cfDNA by methylation-specific PCR with high-resolution melting (HRM), with GAPDH as an endogenous control. Performance was evaluated following CLSI EP05-A3, EP07, EP12-A2, and EP37. Precision of quantification cycle (C<sub>q</sub>) and melting peak temperature (T<sub>m</sub>) was assessed by variance-component analysis within one site and across two sites and two operators. Because precision studies used bulk bisulfite-converted reference DNA, the reported coefficients of variation (CVs) primarily characterize the PCR-HRM detection module; end-to-end variability in clinical plasma specimens may be higher. Interference and cross-reactivity were evaluated in low-positive and contrived-negative samples against reproducibility-derived limits, with dose-response testing of reactive substances. Detection was 100% at both levels, and every run met control-validity criteria. C<sub>q</sub> repeatability CVs ranged from 0.53% to 1.68%, and total reproducibility CVs ranged from 1.10% to 2.37%; all T<sub>m</sub> CVs were ≤0.20%. All 18 interferents and 16 microbial cross-reactants evaluated in low-positive samples met the predefined acceptance criteria. In negative samples, hemoglobin, SARS-CoV-2, and measles virus produced concentration-dependent non-specific amplification, and dose-response testing established their respective no-effect concentrations. These findings characterize the analytical precision and multisite reproducibility of the PCR-HRM detection module and the analytical specificity of MLDx-s, complementing its previously reported clinical performance for plasma-based HCC detection.

title: A quick guide to select pediatric vaccine-preventable diseases
summary:
Purpose of review

Resurgent outbreaks and declining childhood vaccination coverage have amplified the need for pediatricians to promptly recognize and manage vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs). This review summarizes the epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, initial management, public health reporting, and prevention of selected VPDs relevant to pediatric practice.

Recent findings

Childhood vaccination coverage has declined in recent years, coinciding with renewed outbreaks and continued transmission of measles, mumps, pertussis, meningococcal disease, and hepatitis B in the United States. Recent federal immunization schedule changes for children and adolescents (e.g., revised hepatitis B birth-dose guidance, altered meningococcal vaccine decision-making, and expanded pentavalent meningococcal vaccine options) highlight the need for pediatricians to remain familiar with evolving vaccine recommendations.

Summary

Although routine immunization has dramatically reduced the burden of many VPDs, recent declines in vaccine coverage and notable outbreaks have renewed the need for clinical vigilance. Pediatricians should be prepared to identify characteristic presentations, implement appropriate isolation and infection-control measures, obtain timely diagnostic testing, initiate treatment or postexposure management when indicated, and reinforce vaccination as the cornerstone of prevention. This review provides a practical guide to the recognition and management of measles, mumps, pertussis, meningococcal disease, and hepatitis B in pediatric settings.

title: Adverse Events Following Varicella-Containing Vaccination in Healthy Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
summary: Background: Varicella-containing vaccines have substantially reduced the burden of varicella worldwide; however, comprehensive evidence on adverse events following vaccination in children remains important for vaccine safety monitoring, vaccine confidence and immunization policy. We aimed to systematically evaluate the incidence of adverse events following licensed varicella-containing vaccination in healthy children. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating monovalent varicella vaccines or measles-mumps-rubella-varicella (MMRV) vaccines in healthy children aged ≥12 months and <12 years. Eight databases were searched from 1 January 2000 to 17 July 2026. Studies using active safety monitoring and reporting extractable adverse event counts with corresponding denominators were included. Pooled incidence proportions among vaccinated children were estimated using generalized linear mixed models with random effects. Subgroup analyses were performed by vaccine type, vaccination dose, and World Health Organization region. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Results: Forty-three RCTs involving 31,915 vaccinated children were included. Fever was the most frequently reported common adverse event, with a pooled incidence of 11.58% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6.79-19.07%). Pooled incidences were 2.74% (95% CI, 1.10-6.67%) for redness/erythema, 2.19% (95% CI, 0.93-5.06%) for pain, and 0.82% (95% CI, 0.33-1.98%) for swelling. Compared with monovalent varicella vaccines, MMRV vaccines showed higher pooled incidences of fever (43.44% vs. 5.29%), redness/erythema (16.50% vs. 0.69%), pain (12.27% vs. 0.91%), and swelling (7.02% vs. 0.30%); however, these estimates were based on between-study comparisons and should not be interpreted as causal effects of vaccine type. Rare serious adverse events were uncommon, including febrile seizures (0.0989%) and anaphylaxis (0.0343%), with no observed cases of encephalitis. Conclusions: Varicella-containing vaccines were generally well tolerated in children, with most observed adverse events being uncommon and rare serious adverse events infrequently reported. Continued safety surveillance remains important, particularly for rare serious adverse events.

title: Metabolic scaling in a freshwater predator is robust across wild and hatchery-reared populations and experimental designs
summary: Standard metabolic rate (SMR) and maximum metabolic rate (MMR) define the energetic limits of aerobic metabolism in fishes and are increasingly recognized as flexible traits linked to life history variation. Yet the factors driving intraspecific variation in how SMR and MMR scale with body mass and temperature remain unresolved. We assessed mass- and temperature-scaling relationships in SMR, MMR and aerobic scope of walleye (Sander vitreus) using data from multiple intermittent-flow respirometry experiments conducted from 2020 to 2025. The dataset included wild fish from Lake Erie, Lake Ontario, and Rice Lake, and hatchery-reared individuals of Lake Ontario origin (n = 207). Additional MMR<sub>Swim</sub> estimates from swim tunnel respirometry (n = 33) were compared with MMR<sub>Recovery</sub> estimates obtained from a chase and air exposure protocol. Together, body mass and temperature explained 94.7% of the variation in SMR and 80.2% of variation in MMR across the 1-24.5°C range. Sex effects on SMR and MMR were negligible, and apparent differences between populations largely reflected differences in temperature ranges sampled rather than intrinsic population-level differences. Among wild fish (0.36-3.74 kg), SMR scaled hypoallometrically (b = 0.919), whereas hatchery fish, which were relatively smaller, were slightly hyperallometric (b = 1.081). Mass scaling of MMR<sub>Recovery</sub> was shallower (b = 0.664) and consistent with MMR<sub>Swim</sub> (b = 0.682). Our findings suggest that metabolic scaling in walleye is largely conserved across populations in the Laurentian Great Lakes, supporting single-population estimates for regional-scale bioenergetics models used to predict consumption and growth under climate warming.

title: Assessing the Risk for Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak and Health System Response Capacity in Conflict-Affected Sudan
summary:
Background:

Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) is a severe viral hemorrhagic fever with high case fatality rates. Ongoing regional outbreaks in Uganda and the DRC, combined with protracted armed conflict in Sudan since April 2023, increase vulnerability to importation and spread, putting Sudan at risk. Conflict has caused widespread health infrastructure destruction, healthcare worker displacement, and disruption of surveillance and laboratory systems. This study assesses Sudan’s risk of an EVD outbreak and national response capacity in the context of conflict.

Methods:

We reviewed peer-reviewed and grey literature using PubMed, Medline, Google Scholar, WHO, CDC, UNICEF, and UN OCHA reports. No time restrictions were applied. We applied a SWOT analysis framework to classify factors influencing EVD prevention, detection, preparedness, and response in conflict-affected Sudan. The analysis focused on health system functionality, surveillance, laboratory capacity, workforce, and population vulnerabilities.

Results:

Our study found existing strengths, including availability of national EVD preparedness plans, prior experience responding to cholera, dengue, measles, and COVID-19, functional coordination through the Health Cluster, and ongoing disease surveillance systems including EWARS and Event-Based Surveillance. Weaknesses identified include severe disruption of health services (48% of facilities fully functional), health workforce shortages and burnout, disruption of laboratory capacity, and surveillance and access constraints in conflict-affected areas of Darfur and Kordofan. The ongoing health security frameworks, including the National Health Policy, National Health Sector Recovery Plan, and regional cross-border initiatives, expansion of digital surveillance, laboratory decentralization efforts, and recent international investments in health system recovery, provide significant opportunities for optimal preparedness and response. Threats identified include continued armed conflict and insecurity, large-scale internal displacement and cross-border mobility, humanitarian access constraints, and funding instability. Geographic risk synthesis indicates Darfur is at the highest risk for delayed detection and silent transmission, Kordofan serves as a transmission corridor, and Khartoum faces the highest risk of urban amplification.

Conclusion:

Sudan faces a moderate to high EVD outbreak risk due to potential virus importation, a conflict-weakened health system, and mass displacement. Key priorities: strengthen EWARS in conflict zones, decentralize laboratory capacity, restore health facilities with strong IPC, build workforce capacity, and adopt mobility-informed preparedness. Peace and international support remain essential for effective EVD response.

title: Updates on the Molecular Classification of Endometrial Carcinoma
summary: The risk of recurrence and metastasis in patients with endometrial carcinoma varies widely, making evaluation of risk in individual patients critically important for planning effective adjuvant treatment. Tumor histotype and grade have been used, along with stage and lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), but suboptimal reproducibility of histotype assignment (especially for high-grade tumors) and tumor grade have made risk assessment challenging. Similarly, single biomarkers such as L1CAM and beta-catenin have shown potential but none have emerged as well-validated and reproducible markers of risk in endometrial carcinoma. This changed with the finding of The Cancer Genome Atlas that there are 4 molecular subtypes of endometrial carcinoma, based on genomic architecture. Subsequently, a clinically applicable approach to endometrial carcinoma molecular subtype has emerged, based on sequencing of POLE to detect a limited number of pathogenic mutations, and immunostaining for mismatch repair (MMR) proteins and p53. This approach places each endometrial carcinoma into one of 4 molecular subtypes (POLEmut, MMRd, p53abn, and no specific molecular profile [NSMP]) that can be reproducibly diagnosed, show excellent concordance between the biopsy and hysterectomy specimen, are of prognostic significance, predict response to specific adjuvant therapies, and can be used to screen for underlying hereditary cancer susceptibility syndromes. Molecular subtype is now integrated into widely used endometrial carcinoma risk assessment guidelines and is a key component of the 2023 update to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging system for endometrial carcinoma. Recently, prognostic refinement of the 4 molecular groups introduces a possible fifth group showing absence of estrogen receptor (ER) expression and/or high histologic grade within the NSMP subtype. We will review the key features of endometrial carcinoma molecular subtypes, focusing on recent advances in molecular subtype diagnosis in practice.

title: HVSnp: A manually curated database of human SNPS associated with viral infections
summary: We developed the "HVSnp: Human Viruses SNP-related database, a curated database". HVSnp is exclusive to the human SNPs studied and related to viral diseases, with manually mined and curated information from public SNP databases and scientific articles. We used MySQL (version 8.0) due to the easy management and the Looker Studio online availability. Among the output information, we have SNP identification, reference, alternative, and risk alleles, chromosome, gene, and gene function, summary, among others. In total, HVSnp contains eighteen viral diseases and 2020 records: Adenovirus (17 SNPs), Chikungunya (7), COVID-19 (314), Cytomegalovirus (54), Dengue (62), Epstein-Barr (54), Hepatitis A (3), Hepatitis B (380), Hepatitis C (166), Herpes (8), Human immunodeficiency virus (479), Papillomavirus (87), Influenza (74), Measles (68), Respiratory syncytial virus (50), Sars-CoV (80), West Nile (68), and Zika (49). As one SNP can be associated with more than one virus, the number of unique SNPs is 1691 and 651 genes. HVSnp has supplementary information obtained in articles for the summary elaboration, which contains the most significant results described in the literature about a possible relationship between SNPs and viruses. The database is available at URL: https://lookerstudio.google.com/s/pGUC7m538gQ.

title: Beyond PD-L1 and HER2: emerging predictive biomarkers in gastroesophageal tumors
summary: Gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA) remains a major cause of cancer morbidity and mortality, with substantial geographic variation and marked inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity. The implementation of predictive biomarkers, including human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2) overexpression/amplification, programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, deficient mismatch repair/high microsatellite instability (dMMR/MSI-H), and claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), has redefined first-line treatment and enabled biomarker-directed therapeutic selection. Nevertheless, most patients eventually progress, reflecting imperfect biomarker performance, spatial and temporal heterogeneity, coexpression patterns, and complex tumor microenvironment (TME) interactions. Beyond PD-L1, emerging biomarkers such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) status, tumor mutational burden (TMB), and transcriptomic immune signatures provide deeper insight into tumor immunogenicity, although their predictive value remains inconsistent. To overcome resistance, novel therapeutic strategies are targeting alternative inhibitory immune checkpoints [cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domain (TIGIT), lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3), and T cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain containing protein 3 (TIM-3)] and costimulatory pathways (e.g. CD137/TNF receptor superfamily member 9; normally named 4-1BB), as well as emerging targets such as B7-H3 and immunoregulatory axes including C-C motif chemokine receptor 8 (CCR8), Dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK1), transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), and prostaglandin E2 receptor 4 (EP4). Concurrently, emerging targetable alterations such as fibroblast growth factor receptor 2b (FGFR2b) and mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (MET) are reshaping precision treatment, whereas next-generation platforms, including bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and adoptive cellular therapies, are expanding therapeutic opportunities beyond conventional targeted approaches. Notably, these advances have been achieved mainly in the advanced disease setting, whereas approaches for localized GEA remain a critical unmet need. Future progress will require a deeper understanding of the tumor-TME interactions, through integrated, longitudinal, and multidimensional biomarker frameworks that capture genomic, transcriptomic, and immune contexture, alongside adaptive trial designs and equitable access to molecular testing and targeted therapies, to refine precision oncology and improve outcomes in this biologically complex disease.

title: Computational Analysis of the Homologous Mouse Double RINGs Interface for Targeted Anticancer Drug Design
summary: Background/Objectives: The new yearly 1.1 million cancer cases and considerably increasing mortality, after decades of decline, require urgent and effective therapy. Targeted anticancer therapy is an attractive strategy for treating cancer by targeting critical receptors. The MDM2-MDMX RING heterodimer downregulates the p53 tumor suppressor pathway, making its disruption a primary therapeutic strategy in oncology. This study evaluates a series of novel inhibitors against the MDM2-MDMX RING interface to identify potent candidates that overcome the binding affinity and structural stability limitations of current small-molecule options like HLI373. Methods: Comprehensive computational simulations and MM/PBSA energy calculations were performed on five inhibitor complexes: Hinokiflavone, MMRi62, MMRi64, MMRi71, and HLI373. Structural stability, flexibility, and compactness were rigorously analyzed across a 200 ns molecular dynamics simulation trajectory using Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) and Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF) metrics alongside Principal Component Analysis. Results: Among the evaluated MDM2-MDMX dual inhibitors, MMRi62 demonstrated the strongest binding affinity with a ΔGbind of -26.42 kcal/mol, outperforming reference HLI373 (-14.09 kcal/mol), Hinokiflavone (-22.69 kcal/mol), and MMRi64 (-16.73 kcal/mol). Structurally, MMRi64-bound complexes exhibited the highest stability, achieving the lowest RMSD of 2.28 Å and RMSF of 1.30 Å. Conversely, HLI373-bound complexes displayed pronounced structural fluctuations, yielding a high RMSD of 5.11 Å. Conclusions: These inhibitors present highly promising alternatives to HLI373 for targeting the MDM2-MDMX RING interface. MMRi62 and Hinokiflavone, in particular, stand out as highly potent dual-inhibitor leads for future targeted anticancer therapy development.

title: Changing Measles Epidemiology in Ghana, 2018-2023: Exploring Impact of COVID-19-Related Disruptions on Vaccination Coverage and Incidence
summary: Background: Measles remains a public health threat in Ghana due to persistent immunity gaps and suboptimal vaccination coverage. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted routine immunization and may have altered measles transmission. This study assessed measles burden, vaccination status of confirmed cases, and spatiotemporal trends in Ghana, and examined the pandemic's impact on measles control. Methods: We analyzed measles cases reported in Ghana from 2018 to 2023, including age, sex, vaccination status, and region, alongside national measles-rubella (MR) vaccination coverage. Cumulative incidence was calculated as confirmed cases per million population. Interrupted time series analysis assessed pandemic-related disruptions in vaccination coverage and case reporting. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with infection and vaccination status. Results: Ghana reported 1688 confirmed measles cases, a cumulative incidence of 51.9 per million, with a case fatality rate of 0.1%. Incidence rose from 1.1 per 1,000,000 in 2018 to 28.3 per 1,000,000 in 2023, with wide geographic variation. The odds of measles infection were higher among those aged 5-14 years (aOR = 1.41; 95% CI: 1.19-1.68, p < 0.001) and 15-44 years (aOR = 1.74; 95% CI: 1.37-2.22, p < 0.001) than among infants under one year. Compared with no vaccination, one dose was associated with lower odds of measles infection (aOR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.34-0.48, p < 0.001), as was two doses (aOR = 0.38; 95% CI: 0.33-0.44, p < 0.001). MR1 coverage fell from 91.7% to 86.2%, and MR2 coverage stayed below the 95% herd immunity threshold throughout, with both showing an inverse relationship with incidence. The COVID-19 pandemic caused an immediate 64% decline in confirmed cases (IRR 0.36, 95%CI 0.17-0.75, p = 0.007). MR2 coverage dropped 3.66 percentage points at pandemic onset while MR1 rose slightly; neither change was significant. Conclusions: Measles burden in Ghana rose substantially between 2018 and 2023, with geographic variation and an inverse relationship between MR coverage and incidence. Suboptimal two-dose coverage and pandemic disruptions sustained transmission despite vaccination's protective effect. Strengthening routine immunization and surveillance during emergencies is critical to detect outbreaks early and achieve measles elimination.
